b.x: The box does not replace a course or the ambulance. In Brazil: 192, 193, 190. Outside Brazil, the numbers are different. Medicine only what the doctor already prescribed for someone who lives there. A tourniquet goes in only if someone in the house took the course and knows when to loosen it — and even then 192 is in charge. The list to tick, item by item, is in Kits.

One place only, known to whoever lives in the house, including whoever arrives at night. Hall or kitchen, at hand height, not the back of the high cupboard. The same box in the car, smaller, because the crash does not wait for you to come home. In the 72-hour bag, a third, lean. Three boxes, the same logic. Not seven kits scattered that nobody finds. A label on the outside, no skull drawing. Whoever searches in the dark reads with the hand.

Gloves, several pairs. Gauze and a bandage to press the bleeding, another cloth on top if it soaks. Tape. Saline to wash a wound and an eye. Blunt scissors. A plaster and antiseptic for the small cut. Tweezers. An elastic bandage and a triangular cloth, to hold, not to put a bone back. A thermometer. A mouth barrier, if you took the course and will give breaths. A blanket. A pad, which also holds blood and does not call an audience. A notebook and a pencil: the hour it started, the allergy, what you already did. Ink dies in water. Sugar or pocket glucose only for someone who is awake and swallows. A written card: 192, 193, 190, the insurance, the house allergy. Paper. Not a QR code.
The medicine that belongs to the house

A painkiller you already use, with the name the doctor knows. A two-week reserve of the daily medicine: pressure, diabetes, thyroid, the child’s, with the dose written and the expiry. Epinephrine and an inhaler only if they were prescribed, and whoever uses them knows which box they are in. Do not buy an antibiotic on your own. Do not keep the expired tablet “because one day”. Do not mix the bottle with no label. The corner pharmacy closes on the holiday and in the flood. What is not in the box this Tuesday does not exist on Thursday.

A scalpel, sewing thread, a needle to pierce a wound. That is not a kit. It is fantasy. A war tourniquet does not go into the box of someone who never trained the turn. Alcohol on a deep wound is not the plan. Ice on a burn is not the plan. A colored ointment without knowing what it is is not the plan. Twelve items with an English name that nobody in the house opens. If a child exists, the child’s box exists: the right dose, saline, a thermometer. If not, do not fill it with baby things to look complete.

After a flood, what is missing most is not a tourniquet. It is soap, a way to wash the hand, oral rehydration if the family doctor already advised it, and repellent because dengue and leptospirosis arrive before hunger. In the heat of the car, ointment and plaster melt: the vehicle box stays in the shade, and you look at the expiry on the same day you look at the oil. A torn glove leaves. Opened gauze leaves. What expired leaves on Tuesday, with the pantry clock. Do not wait for the cut to discover the bandage turned to dust.
The box only counts if the hand has already opened it

Once a month, open it. See whether the gauze is in place, whether the glove has not torn, whether the pressure medicine still holds, whether the number card did not get wet. Whoever does not live alone has to find the box with eyes closed. The lesson teaches the gesture. The red tab is the lookup when someone has already fallen. The kit is the cloth, the glove, and the pencil between the two. Without that, the knowledge stays on the screen and the bleeding stays on the shirt.
